items.desc: Social media communication on online travel platforms may contribute to customer well-being when it encourages participation and positive emotional experiences, according to a study of 210 Generation Z users reported in the International Journal of Electronic Marketing and Retailing.

items.title: Long-term analysis questions whether Japan's depopulation policy can stabilize shrinking communities
items.desc: Small and medium-sized cities (SMCs) are essential for balanced national development, yet many are now facing prolonged population loss, aging and weakened labor markets. Japan has addressed this challenge for more than half a century through the Depopulated-Area-Designation (DAD) policy, a national framework that identifies municipalities facing population loss and supports them through infrastructure, fiscal, industrial and social measures. However, it has not been determined whether such a designation can stabilize shrinking communities over time.

items.title: Global happiness researchers reveal keys to a good life
items.desc: Many of the world's leading happiness researchers say they consciously spend more time with loved ones after seeing the evidence, according to a new paper. "Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it," says Lara Aknin, a professor of social psychology at Simon Fraser University.

items.title: False lingzhi unmasked: Scientists crack the 245-year mystery behind a medicinal mushroom mix-up
items.desc: In a new study published today in Plants, People, Planet, scientists from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, and their international collaborators clarify the distinction between Ganoderma lucidum, a European bracket fungus described in 1781, and Ganoderma lingzhi, the East Asian species widely associated with medicinal lingzhi or reishi.

items.title: Students' love-hate relationship with AI
items.desc: ChatGPT hit like a meteorite in late 2022 and found fertile ground at EPFL, invading the computers and smartphones of tomorrow's engineers. Within two years, generative AI had spread like wildfire among our students owing to their still-malleable learning habits and the growing number of models—and the many improvements to them.

items.title: Zoologist's study of wild Panamanian bats highlights use of metrics to inform bat conservation
items.desc: Bats are not only a marvel of myth and imagination but also of energy use, working at the height of their energetic ceiling to fly the night skies the world over.

items.title: New online tool to help turn food waste into opportunity
items.desc: Western Australian businesses can now make better-informed decisions about reducing food waste and turning discarded materials into valuable products, thanks to a new online toolkit.

items.title: Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it
items.desc: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.

items.title: A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
items.desc: A solar eclipse recorded more than 2,700 years ago is revealing surprising secrets about Earth's rotation and the Sun's ancient behavior. By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital, scientists were able to reconstruct a total solar eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and obtain more accurate measurements of how fast Earth was spinning at the time.

items.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
items.desc: Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.

items.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck
items.desc: A mysterious shipwreck off Turkey’s coast may be the oldest ever discovered, dating back approximately 4,500 years to the age of the Egyptian pyramids. Although the wooden vessel has disappeared, its surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations. Researchers believe the ship may have crashed against rocks during a storm while transporting valuable goods such as oil, wine, or tree resin.

items.title: Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
items.desc: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

items.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
items.desc: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

items.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
items.desc: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

items.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
items.desc: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.

items.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
items.desc: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.

items.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
items.desc: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.

items.title: A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
items.desc: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.

items.title: Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
items.desc: Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it.

items.title: NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
items.desc: Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.

items.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
items.desc: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
items.desc: A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others.

items.title: Lula Killed the Donroe Doctrine
items.desc: In attempting to disentangle the United States from the rest of the world and retreat into a seemingly controllable hemispheric stronghold, Donald Trump's Latin America strategy had fared better than the rest of his foreign policy. But following a defeat for the far right in Brazil, his project now looks dead in the water.

items.title: The Wrong Way to Compare Economic Size
items.desc: At the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, Paul Krugman concluded that, when it comes to “weaponized interdependence,” the EU is more powerful than both the US and China. But his reliance on PPP-adjusted GDP as a way to smooth out the volatility of nominal exchange rates ignores the even greater swings in PPP data.

items.title: Public Control for a Purposeful Economy
items.desc: As more governments recognize the need for greater public control over economic outcomes, they must be careful to define the concept well. What ultimately matters is not ownership, but the state’s capacity to steer economic activity toward strategic objectives in the service of the common good.

items.title: Rethinking Sustainable Livelihoods From the Ground Up
items.desc: In regions where economic activity has long revolved around fossil-fuel extraction, ensuring a just transition requires developing alternative livelihoods that account for each community’s specific needs. Regional endowment funds could be a useful vehicle for funding these local initiatives.

items.title: The Specter of an AI-Driven Slowdown
items.desc: The rush to finance AI infrastructure is driving up borrowing costs just as governments grapple with mounting debt and persistent fiscal deficits. If the AI investment boom falters, falling valuations could choke off financing, with little room for fiscal and monetary policy to cushion the economic shock.

items.title: Is a Chinese Implosion Looming?
items.desc: If current trends continue, the Chinese state will find itself exposed to a political succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. It would be a perfect storm, with far-reaching global repercussions.

This is true of the global trading system, which has proven surprisingly resilient in recent years, and of the European economy, which might not have a tech giant to rival those in the US or China, but remains a global trade powerhouse and a leader in science and research. items.desc: Civil-society oversight is the cheapest insurance in sovereign finance, because it enables independent scrutiny long before a default. But given that a borrowing government will never volunteer to fund the people who audit it, global decision-makers must do so using agreements for stolen-asset recovery and sovereign-debt treatments.

items.title: How to Help Left-Behind Regions
items.desc: Pouring public investment into poorer towns and cities might be politically beneficial, but the economic returns of indiscriminate largesse would be limited. A better approach would concentrate investment in areas with the potential to become high-productivity hubs, such as large peripheral cities.

items.title: The Agentic Information Economy
items.desc: An internet populated and run by AI agents will need not just reliable data but also a broader information ecology capable of questioning its own inputs and transmitting corrections where they are needed if information changes. But whether this will serve private interests or the public good remains to be seen.

items.title: A Competitive Europe Must Be Climate-Resilient
items.desc: Extreme weather and climate-related events caused €822 billion in economic losses across the European Union between 1980 and 2024, with a quarter of the losses occurring just in the last five years. The consequences for Europe’s competitiveness and economic security are clear—and so is the appropriate response.

items.title: Europe Must Prepare for the Worst
items.desc: Those seeking to weaken the EU’s supranational foundations are already preparing their radical schemes, like the “new deal for Europe” that Germany's Alternative für Deutschland recently presented in the European Parliament. The pro-EU camp must be prepared with new political strategies and institutional arrangements.

items.title: Nature Can’t Wait
items.desc: Although the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are spurring governments to increase spending on defense and focus more on economic growth, it would be a mistake to postpone investments designed to protect nature. In fact, meeting internationally agreed targets could add up to $450 billion to annual global GDP by 2050.

items.title: Argentina’s Economic Chainsaw Massacre
items.desc: Argentine President Javier Milei may currently be a lynchpin in US President Donald Trump’s geoeconomic vision for Latin America; but he could soon become its weak link. With elections coming next year, he has achieved an economic recovery and relative price stability by driving millions of his people into destitution.

items.title: Which AI Myth Will We Embrace?
items.desc: The mythos—or foundational stories—that we tell ourselves will determine our fate in the age of AI. As industry leaders regale us with utopian visions of benevolent digital gods delivering scientific breakthroughs and expanding our technological horizons, our best defense against hubris is a counternarrative of social cooperation.
